proposals.before: Ministers argued that the boy emperor required a regent and urged her to follow the precedent of Han Empress Dowager He.
proposals.after: Ministers argued that the boy emperor required a regent and urged her to follow the precedent of Han Empress Hexi.
proposals.reason: 和熹 is the posthumous title Hexi, not the surname He.

proposals.before: The assembled ministers memorialized: the Son of Heaven is young and tender; it is fitting to follow the precedent of Empress Dowager He of Han.
proposals.after: The assembled ministers memorialized: the Son of Heaven is young and tender; it is fitting to follow the precedent of Empress Hexi of Han.
proposals.reason: Chinese 漢和熹皇后 is Empress Hexi of Han, not Empress He.

proposals.before: Empress Du the Chenggong had the taboo personal name Lingyang; she was a person of Jingzhao and was the great-granddaughter of the General Who Guards the South, Yu.
proposals.after: Empress Du the Chenggong had the taboo personal name Lingyang; she was a person of Jingzhao and was the great-granddaughter of the General Who Guards the South, Du Yu.
proposals.reason: 預 here is Du Yu; the given name alone conceals the identity.

proposals.before: Xuan district's Lingyang county was changed to Guangyang county.
proposals.after: Lingyang county in Xuancheng commandery was changed to Guangyang county.
proposals.reason: 宣城 is Xuancheng commandery, not Xuan district.

proposals.before: Empress Chu the Kangxian (Healthy and Presented).
proposals.reason: 康獻 is the compound posthumous title Kangxian; splitting it into Healthy and Presented is a false etymological gloss.

proposals.before: My late sister-consort was yielding and gentle, ever seeking to follow Earth's way; she deferred to the court's wishes because she put the state first.
proposals.after: The late empress was yielding and gentle, ever seeking to follow Earth's way; she deferred to the court's wishes because she put the state first.
proposals.reason: 先后 means the previous empress, not a sister-consort.

proposals.before: Minister Yin Rong, citing Zheng Xuan, ruled that General Who Guards the Wei Chu Pou should observe full court etiquette inside the palace, but on days when the dowager visited her natal home they might behave as father and daughter.
proposals.after: Minister Yin Rong, citing Zheng Xuan, ruled that General of the Guards Chu Pou should observe full court etiquette inside the palace, but on days when the dowager visited her natal home they might behave as father and daughter.
proposals.reason: 衛將軍 is the Jin office General of the Guards, not a general who guards Wei.

proposals.before: Minister of Ceremonies Yin Rong argued according to Zheng Xuan's meaning: when General Who Guards the Wei Pou was within the palace precincts then full ministerial respect; on days when the Empress Dowager returned to comfort her parents, naturally like family-person rites.
proposals.after: Minister of Ceremonies Yin Rong argued according to Zheng Xuan's meaning: when General of the Guards Pou was within the palace precincts then full ministerial respect; on days when the Empress Dowager returned to comfort her parents, naturally like family-person rites.
proposals.reason: 衛將軍 is General of the Guards; Wei is not a toponym here.

proposals.before: Shang leaned by the door before viewing several lines of the memorial, then said, 'I myself originally suspected this'; reaching halfway then stopped, demanded brush and replied to the memorial saying: 'The not-yet-dead person encounters these hundred griefs; moved in thought for the living and dead, the heart therein is as if cut.'
proposals.after: Still leaning by the door she viewed several lines of the memorial, then said, 'I myself originally suspected this'; reaching halfway then stopped, demanded a brush and replied to the memorial saying: 'The not-yet-dead person encounters these hundred griefs; moved in thought for the living and dead, the heart therein is as if cut.'
proposals.reason: 尚 here is the adverb still, not the personal name Shang; the subject remains the Empress Dowager.

proposals.before: To the emperor she was a cousin's widow, so the court debated what mourning he should wear for her.
proposals.after: To the emperor she was a cousin's wife, so the court debated what mourning he should wear for her.
proposals.reason: 從嫂 names the living kinship (wife of a male cousin), not widowhood; widowhood is only the occasion of the mourning debate.

proposals.before: Her father was Bing; she herself has a biography.
proposals.after: Her father was Bing; he has his own biography.
proposals.reason: 自有傳 refers to the father's separate biography, not to the empress.

proposals.before: The Emperor summoned Wang Bao as Gentleman of the Masters of Writing, thereby to please the empress's intent.
proposals.after: The Emperor summoned Prince Bao as Gentleman of the Masters of Writing, thereby to please the empress's intent.
proposals.reason: 王褒 is Prince Bao (長沙王褒), not a man surnamed Wang; the idiomatic rendering already has Sima Bao.

proposals.before: In the nineteenth year of Taiyuan, Emperor Xiaowu issued an edict saying: 'The Grand Consort of Kuaiji had the virtue of the civil mother; her fine reputation had fusion; she bore and carried sagely brightness; glory extended to Jin.
proposals.after: In the nineteenth year of Taiyuan, Emperor Xiaowu issued an edict saying: 'The Grand Consort of Kuaiji had the virtue of Wenmu; her fair fame endures; she bore sagely brightness; glory extended to Jin.
proposals.reason: 文母 is the Zhou exemplar Wenmu, not a generic civil mother; 徽音有融 is the Shijing idiom that fair fame endures.

proposals.before: She dreamed repeatedly of twin dragons cradled in her lap and of sun and moon sliding into her bosom; she told her companions she took this for a blessing. When the prince heard, he was intrigued—soon she gave birth to the future Emperor Xiaowu, Prince Daozi of Kuaiji, and the elder princess of Poyang.
proposals.after: She dreamed repeatedly of twin dragons cradled in her lap and of sun and moon sliding into her bosom; she told her companions she took this for a blessing. When the prince heard, he was intrigued—soon she gave birth to the future Emperor Xiaowu, Prince Wenxiao of Kuaiji, and the elder princess of Poyang.
proposals.reason: This unit names 会稽文孝王, not 道子; inserting Daozi invents a personal name the sentence does not use.

proposals.before: In the fourth year of Yonghe, mother and son together lost the Emperor's favor; both were secretly deposed; the empress thereupon from grief died.
proposals.after: In the fourth year of Yonghe, mother and son together lost the prince's favor; both were confined and deposed; the empress thereupon died of grief.
proposals.reason: In Yonghe 4 Jianwen was still Prince of Kuaiji, so 帝意 is the prince favor; 幽废 is confinement and deposition.

proposals.before: Empress Wang's personal name was Shen'ai; she came from Linyi in Langya commandery.
proposals.after: Empress Wang the Anxi's personal name was Shen'ai; she came from Linyi in Langya commandery.
proposals.reason: The Chinese title 安僖王皇后 includes the posthumous name Anxi, which the idiomatic English drops.

proposals.before: Renowned for beauty and skill at song and lute, she entered the palace as a Shuyuan lady and bore Emperors An and Gong.
proposals.after: Renowned for beauty and skill at song and lute, she entered the palace as a Shuyuan lady and bore Emperor An and Emperor Gong.
proposals.reason: Emperors An fuses the title and first designation ungrammatically; the Chinese names two emperors, An and Gong.

proposals.before: Lady Feng was slender grace; beauty lush and softly yielding.
proposals.after: Lady Fen was slender grace; beauty lush and softly yielding.
proposals.reason: 芬 is Fen, not Feng; the idiomatic rendering invents a different reading.

proposals.before: Each avoided Huayang's blame; ultimately trod Harmonious and Bright's tracks; preserved decline to achieve end—what was fortunately attained was indeed much.
proposals.after: Each avoided Huayang's blame; ultimately trod Hexi's tracks; preserved decline to achieve end—what was fortunately attained was indeed much.
proposals.reason: 和熹 is the posthumous name Hexi of Deng Sui, not the adjectives Harmonious and Bright.

decisions.reason: The source names 漢和熹皇后, Empress Hexi of Han by posthumous title 和熹; the original English invents a Han empress surnamed He.
漢和熹皇后 is Empress Hexi of Han, not Empress Dowager He; Hexi is the posthumous title, and the title here is 皇后.
The Chinese writes only the given name 預 after the office; the original literal is accurate, and the idiomatic field already supplies Du Yu.
宣城 is Xuancheng commandery; rendering it as Xuan district misreads the place name.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 改宣城陵陽縣為廣陽縣

decisions.reason: 康獻 is the compound posthumous title Kangxian; the parenthetical Healthy and Presented is an invented etymological gloss.
先后 is the previous empress, a court exemplar, not a sister-consort of the speaker.
衛將軍 is the Jin office General of the Guards; Wei is not a territory being guarded.
衛將軍 is General of the Guards, not a general who guards Wei.
尚 is the adverb still; the subject remains the empress dowager who has just come out, not a person named Shang.
從嫂 names the kinship cousin's wife; it does not itself mean widow, even though the mourning debate follows her death.
自有傳 after 父冰 points to the father's separate biography, not to a biography of the empress.
王褒 here is Prince Bao, matching the idiomatic Sima Bao; 王 is the princely title, not the surname Wang.
文母 is the Zhou exemplar Wenmu, not a civil mother, and 徽音有融 is the Shijing idiom that fair fame endures, not fusion.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 會稽太妃文母之德，徽音有融

decisions.reason: The sentence names 會稽文孝王; inserting Daozi adds a personal name this unit does not use.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 遂生孝武帝及會稽文孝王、鄱陽長公主

decisions.reason: In Yonghe 4 she was still Princess Consort of Kuaiji, so 帝意 is her husband's princely favor, and 幽廢 is confinement and deposition, not a secret abdication.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 母子並失帝意，俱被幽廢

decisions.reason: 安僖王皇后 includes the posthumous name Anxi, which the original idiomatic English omits.
Emperors An and Gong is grammatical English for 安、恭二帝; expanding each title is stylistic, not a correction of meaning.

decisions.after: Lady Fen was of slender grace; her beauty lush and softly yielding.
decisions.reason: 芬 is Fen, not Feng, but the proposed sentence remains ungrammatical; the name must be Fen and the English needs a minimal grammar repair.
和熹 is the posthumous name Hexi, not the adjectives Harmonious and Bright.

claimRevisions.reason: The accepted repair shows 衛將軍 is General of the Guards, so the extracted English office label must drop the false toponym reading.
The repaired unit names 芬 as Fen; the extracted title Lady Feng was produced only by the mistranslation.
